topic.refined: Should the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act become law as written — the 10^29-FLOP prohibition on training or running superintelligence-scale models, plus its public-ownership mandate for compute, data, and algorithms, its public dividend, and its whistleblower protections — making this a debate over the political economy of AI rather than just a compute cap? Anchor the normative core first: under deep uncertainty about loss-of-control and concentration-of-power risk, is precautionary prohibition justified against a permissionless-innovation default, and which side bears the burden of proof — labs demonstrating safety before scaling, or regulators demonstrating danger before banning? Then stress-test the bill's five-year moratorium window empirically: given DeepSeek-R1's near-frontier reasoning built on a ~2.8×10^23-FLOP base run, o3-style test-time compute, and distillation putting o1-mini-level AIME performance into 32B-parameter students — set against Epoch AI's measured 4-5×/year frontier training-compute growth and roughly 8-month algorithmic-efficiency doublings — will capability decouple from FLOP counts so quickly that the 10^29 threshold is either obsolete (superhuman-capability models trainable an order of magnitude below the line, saturating benchmarks like GPQA Diamond and SWE-bench Verified) or trivially evadable (distributed training, offshore clusters, unlogged inference) before the moratorium expires? And finally: is the bill's implicit thesis correct — that AI's binding danger is a handful of firms monopolizing compute, data, and capital, which public ownership and a dividend address better than any FLOP speed limit?

questions.question: Should the debate center on the desirability of the prohibition itself, or on the feasibility of its specific enforcement design?
options: Desirability: whether prohibiting training runs above 10^26 FLOPs (roughly 5x the estimated compute for GPT-4) is net-positive given existential-risk arguments versus forgone capabilities in science and medicine.

Enforceability: whether FLOP-based thresholds can be monitored at scale, given distributed training, compute-rental arbitrage across jurisdictions, and ambiguities in FLOP accounting for training runs.

Institutional design: whether an OSHA-style oversight division, a licensing tier for 10^25-10^26 FLOP models, and criminal penalties up to 20 years avoid regulatory capture and the information asymmetries between agency and frontier labs.
Whole-bill scope: including the public-ownership, dividend, and whistleblower provisions, so the debate covers the political economy of AI rather than only the ban provision.

questions.question: Is the core disagreement you most want to surface empirical, normative, or definitional?
options: Empirical: whether compute scale is a valid proxy for dangerous capability, drawing on scaling-law evidence and the disputed emergence literature (Wei et al. 2022 vs. Schaeffer et al. 2023's mirage critique), versus eval-based alternatives to FLOP thresholds.
Normative: whether precautionary prohibition under deep uncertainty is justified against a permissionless-innovation default, and which side bears the burden of proof.
Definitional: whether 'superintelligence' is coherently operationalized by compute thresholds at all, versus capability benchmark ceilings or agentic-autonomy criteria.

Threat-model dependent: the bill implicitly invokes loss-of-control and concentration-of-power risks, and the debate could test which threat models actually support a ban versus narrower, targeted interventions.

questions.question: What timeframe and stakeholder lens should anchor the debate?
options: Near-term (2025-2028): how the ban would affect frontier labs currently planning multi-gigawatt training clusters that approach the 10^26 FLOP threshold.

The five-year moratorium window: whether algorithmic efficiency gains will decouple capability from FLOP counts, rendering the threshold either obsolete or trivially evadable within the bill's own horizon.
Long-run existential: whether a temporary ban materially changes cumulative existential risk versus merely shifting development timelines and geography.
Geopolitical: whether a unilateral US prohibition cedes frontier advantage to China, or whether export-control-style enforcement and the existing compute gap make unilateral limits robust.
